To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the climate projections suggest that water availability in Nigeria will increase for about half of the country in the future and that, for more of the country, storage investment decisions should not be made using historical data.

(i) climate projections are uncertain, but they converge in projecting increase in water flows in the future for almost half of Nigeria; (ii) the lack of agreement among different projections on precipitation and inflows makes it difficult to predict how much water will effectively be available in the future, especially for the most water-scarce areas; (iii) the risk of designing reservoirs that are not suitable for the future climate is high, especially in the most water-scare areas.

(i) the climate projections for Nigeria are uncertain; (ii) the projections of water availability are uncertain; and (iii) the design of reservoirs based only on historical data may lead to over- or underdesigning of reservoirs.

The main takeaway from our work is that

climate change is likely to impact on the design and management of water resources infrastructure, and that a better understanding of the potential impacts of climate change on the hydrological regime is necessary to support water resources management and planning.
the risk of under-designing future storage is not negligible and that the use of historical data to design future storage might lead in some cases to excessive capital outlays.
the design of future investments for irrigation in Nigeria should be supported by a robust analysis of the range of future climate outcomes.
